title: India Launches First-Ever Guide to Grasslands and Other Open Natural Ecosystems at UNCCD COP17, in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia
subtitle:
Union Environment Minister stresses the need for Science-based Conservation of Open Natural Ecosystems alongside Forests
Healthy Grasslands are indispensable for Biodiversity, Livelihoods and Climate Resilience: Shri Bhupender Yadav
body_text:
India launched its first-ever Guide to Grasslands and Other Open Natural Ecosystems (ONEs) of India at the 17th Session of the Conference of the Parties (COP17) to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) in Ulaanbaatar (Mongolia), on 17.08.2026. The document highlights the rich diversity, ecological significance and socio-economic importance of India’s grasslands, savannas, deserts and other open natural ecosystems. It marks an important step towards strengthening their conservation, restoration and sustainable management.
The launch was preceded by a special video message from Shri Bhupender Yadav, Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Government of India. He informed that grasslands, scrublands and ravines have for too long been judged by the absence of trees, despite these ecosystems sheltering species found nowhere else on earth and sustaining pastoral communities. He said modern science reinforces the understanding of local communities that healthy grasslands are indispensable for biodiversity, livelihoods and climate resilience.
Virtually addressed the side event on the launch of the first-ever Guide to Grasslands and Other Open Natural Ecosystems (ONEs) of India at the UNCCD COP17 in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia today. Highlighted the diversity and distribution of India’s grasslands and open natural… pic.twitter.com/t5LMvVfZpH — Bhupender Yadav (@byadavbjp) August 17, 2026
Shri Yadav said the Guide was close to his heart as he grew up in Ajmer, Rajasthan, surrounded by grazing lands and desert scrub that were often described as “wasteland”. Recalling the traditional Oran or gauchar landscapes protected by villages, he said local communities understood that land, herds and their own lives were closely interconnected.
The Minister described the Guide as an important step towards recognising India’s open natural ecosystems and stressed the need for their science-based conservation alongside forests. He hoped it would inspire greater understanding and conservation of these ecosystems.
The Guide was launched at an official UNCCD COP17 side event under the aegis and guidance of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEF&CC), Government of India. The publication of the Guide and the event was organised by the Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment (ATREE) in collaboration with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), Centre of Excellence on Sustainable Land Management (CoE-SLM), Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education (ICFRE), and Space Applications Centre (SAC), ISRO. It brought together representatives from Government, scientific and research institutions, international organisations and civil society.
Presentations and discussions highlighted the diversity and distribution of India’s grasslands and ONEs, their ecological importance, and the role of their restoration in achieving India’s Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) targets. The need for stronger scientific knowledge, improved land-degradation assessment and landscape-level planning was also emphasised.
The Guide brings together information on major Open Natural Ecosystems across India, covering their geographical settings, ecological characteristics, biodiversity, and the communities and tribes associated with them. It also contains thematic sections on pastoralism, fire ecology and carbon sequestration. India’s ONEs range from Himalayan and Terai grasslands to the Thar and Banni landscapes, Deccan savannas, rocky plateaus, ravines, scrublands, coastal ecosystems and desert landscapes. These ecosystems support diverse biodiversity, contribute to soil and water processes, store substantial carbon in their soils, and sustain pastoral, livestock-based and agricultural livelihoods.
The event also featured two fireside chats with national and international experts, scientific institutions, civil society and community-focused organisations. Discussions focused on grassland and dryland conservation and restoration, people-centred rangeland governance, climate resilience, and the institutional, scientific and policy measures needed for landscape-scale conservation and sustainable management of ONEs.
The launch reaffirmed India’s commitment to a science-informed and landscape-based approach to land restoration and sustainable land management. It underscored the need to bring grasslands, rangelands and other open natural ecosystems into mainstream discussions on land degradation, biodiversity conservation, climate resilience and sustainable livelihoods.
The Guide is expected to serve as a valuable resource for policymakers, researchers, conservation practitioners, development agencies and communities working towards the conservation, restoration and sustainable management of India’s grasslands and other ONEs. Its launch at COP17 also provides an important platform for India to showcase its diverse open ecosystems and strengthen their representation in the global discourse on land restoration, rangelands and Land Degradation Neutrality.

ministry.name: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

enrichment.summary: India launched its first-ever 'Guide to Grasslands and Other Open Natural Ecosystems (ONEs) of India' at the UNCCD COP17 in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, on 17 August 2026. Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav virtually addressed the launch event, emphasizing science-based conservation of grasslands, savannas, deserts and other open ecosystems alongside forests. The Guide, produced under MoEF&CC's guidance by ATREE with IUCN, CoE-SLM, ICFRE and ISRO's Space Applications Centre, documents India's grassland ecosystems—from Himalayan and Terai grasslands to the Thar, Banni and Deccan savannas—covering their biodiversity, associated communities, pastoralism, fire ecology and carbon sequestration.
enrichment.context:
India's grasslands, scrublands, ravines and deserts have historically been classified as 'wastelands' in revenue and land-use records because they lack tree cover, leading to their conversion for agriculture, industry or afforestation drives that often ignore their ecological value. This has undermined conservation of species like the Great Indian Bustard and habitats crucial to pastoral communities practicing traditional grazing-based livelihoods, such as the Oran/gauchar systems of Rajasthan. Ecologists have long argued that Open Natural Ecosystems (ONEs) are distinct, ancient biomes with unique biodiversity and carbon storage in soil rather than biomass, and deserve conservation frameworks separate from forest-centric afforestation policy.

The launch is tied to India's commitments under the UNCCD, particularly Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) targets, which India adopted voluntarily to restore degraded land by 2030. UNCCD COP sessions are a key platform for showcasing India's land restoration initiatives, alongside other efforts like the Bonn Challenge pledge to restore 26 million hectares of degraded land. This Guide is significant as an official government-backed document that formally recognizes grasslands and ONEs as ecologically valuable landscapes requiring dedicated science-based management, potentially influencing future land classification, restoration funding and policy at the national level.

prelims_questions.question: 'Open Natural Ecosystems (ONEs)' as referred to in India's newly launched Guide include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Tropical rainforests of the Western Ghats
prelims_questions.explanation: The Guide covers grasslands, savannas, deserts, scrublands, ravines and coastal ecosystems as Open Natural Ecosystems; dense tropical rainforests are not classified under ONEs, which are specifically non-forest, open landscapes.

prelims_questions.question: The UNCCD COP17, at which India launched its Guide to Grasslands and Other Open Natural Ecosystems, was held in which country?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states the COP17 session was held in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, in August 2026.
